title: An elementary upper bound for vector-addition-system reachability
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing-machine algorithm A and fixed integers h≥0 and c≥1 such that, for every explicitly encoded vector-addition-system reachability instance of bit length N, A decides exact reachability correctly within E_h((N+2)^c) steps, where E_0(x)=x and E_{j+1}(x)=2^{E_j(x)}? The constants and the single algorithm must work for all input dimensions and numerical values. This historical proposition is false.

source_formulation.text: Despite intense investigation during the last four decades, it is still an open problem whether an elementary complexity upper bound for the reachability problem exists.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

why: Exact resource reachability is a basic verification problem that other decision tasks can encode. Its non-elementary complexity shows that decidability can coexist with worst-case costs beyond every fixed-height exponential tower, and that exact target matching can be much harder than merely accumulating enough resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The elementary-upper-bound proposition is false by the STOC 2019 / JACM 2021 non-elementarity result of Czerwiński, Lasota, Lazić, Leroux and Mazowiecki. The accepted journal manuscript’s Section 1 model and Theorem 6 match the unrestricted VAS reachability question on the original 2018 page. The later Ackermann-completeness result strengthens this resolution. Source and theorem matching were checked; proofs were not independently audited or formalized.

progress.text: Leroux records the elementary-upper-bound question for general vector addition systems in the introduction.
Czerwiński and coauthors present the non-elementary lower bound at STOC, answering this question negatively.
The non-elementarity result appears in Journal of the ACM, volume 68, article 7.
Czerwiński and Orlikowski establish the matching Ackermann hardness classification, independently of Leroux’s lower-bound work; the checked full-text revision is from October 2022.
The MFCS branching-VASS paper distinguishes the settled ordinary reachability complexity from its branching generalization.

sentences: A vector addition system repeatedly adds permitted integer vectors while keeping every counter nonnegative.
Exact reachability asks whether a given initial vector can reach a specified target after finitely many such steps.
The historical question asks whether one algorithm can decide all instances within a fixed-height tower of exponentials in the input length.
The non-elementary lower bound published at STOC 2019 and in JACM 2021 rules out every such bound.
The card therefore records a resolved negative answer, with the general model kept separate from the polynomial-growth subclass named in the original paper.

importance.reason: Importance has not been individually assessed. This draft shares the provisional midpoint with other unassessed drafts; its position is not evidence that the question is less important.

definitions: An instance is a dimension d≥1, a nonempty finite list T of displacement vectors in ℤ^d, and initial and target vectors a,b∈ℕ^d, with ℕ={0,1,2,…}. A configuration is any vector in ℕ^d. From u one may take displacement t∈T exactly when every coordinate of u+t is nonnegative, obtaining u+t. The target is reachable if a finite sequence t₁,…,t_k∈T has a+∑_{i=1}^j t_i∈ℕ^d for every 0≤j≤k and a+∑_{i=1}^k t_i=b. Length k=0 is allowed. The input explicitly lists all coordinates, using binary integers with signs and separators; N is the total bit length. Dimension and list length are input parameters. A is one finite deterministic program and must halt with the exact yes/no answer on every valid instance. No random error, counter bound, polynomial-growth promise, zero-test instruction, or branching operation is included. An elementary running-time bound has some fixed tower height h as defined in the statement; the height cannot depend on the instance. Binary encoding fixes the presentation without changing whether any elementary bound exists, since translation to unary data has at most elementary size growth.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute existence of the single uniform elementary-time decision algorithm quantified above. A refutation must exclude every fixed tower height and polynomial bottom exponent; showing that one algorithm or one fixed resource bound fails is insufficient. The published non-elementary lower bound supplies the negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: A counter vector can describe the quantities of several resources in a concurrent system. Every transition makes a fixed change, but cannot consume resources that are absent. The reachability question asks whether the system can finish with exactly the specified quantities, after any finite number of transitions.

For example, start at (2,0) with the single displacement (−1,2). The reachable vectors are (2,0), (1,2) and (0,4). The target (0,3) is not reachable, although (0,4) is coordinatewise at least as large. Replacing exact equality by that weaker comparison gives coverability, a different task.

Polynomial time, exponential time and a fixed stack of several exponentials are all elementary. Allowing the stack height to grow with input size is a qualitatively stronger resource bound. The old question asked whether some fixed height would suffice for every instance, rather than whether a particular implementation could be made faster.

The quoted 2018 question concerns unrestricted vector addition systems. The paper’s title refers to a special polynomial-growth subclass studied later in the article; imposing that restriction here would change the question. Likewise, a bound for one fixed low dimension would not establish the required uniform bound over all dimensions.

Czerwiński and coauthors proved a lower bound excluding elementary complexity, first presented at STOC 2019 and developed in a 2021 journal article. This is a limitation of the decision problem itself, not merely a demonstration of long runs or poor performance by an existing algorithm.

Subsequent work classified ordinary VAS/VASS reachability as Ackermann-complete. Finite control states and the state-free vector presentation are polynomially interreducible, so this later classification concerns the same unrestricted reachability task. The simpler non-elementarity theorem already settles the historical yes/no question recorded here.
